The building itself is the old Board School annexe, leased from the town council for a peppercorn
rent on a lease that runs to 2047. It has a strong room that was once the coal store, a workroom that
was once a classroom, and a reading room that still has the pegs for coats along one wall. Nobody
has ever suggested removing the pegs, and nobody should; they are the last of the original fittings,
and the caretaker, who has been here longer than the archive, is fond of them.

Volunteers new to cataloguing shadow an experienced hand for their first three boxes and are then
left to work alone, with the understanding that the first ten entries anyone writes will be read by
somebody else before they are filed. That reading is a conversation, not an inspection. Most of what
it catches is not error but habit: a tendency to guess at dates, to write scope notes as though the
reader already knew the family, or to let an interesting letter distract from the dull ledger that
actually tells the story of the box far better than the letter does. The habit is harmless in a reader
and expensive in a cataloguer. Neither is a fault in the person.

provenance.key:
Cataloguing is the slow heart of the work, and it is deliberately separated from intake so that
neither hurries the other. A box may wait a year between the accession log and its catalogue entry.
That is acceptable. What is not acceptable is a box that has been partly described, because a partial
description looks complete to anyone who did not write it, and the missing half is then invisible for
a generation. Finish a box or leave it plainly marked as untouched; there is no useful state in
between, and no shame in the second.

The catalogue entry for a box has four parts: a reference number, a title, a date range and a scope
note. The reference follows the accession, so it is fixed before the box is opened. The title is the
depositor's own name for the material where one exists and a plain description where one does not.
The date range is taken from the documents themselves and never guessed. The scope note says
what kind of material the box contains and, briefly, what it is about, in that order.

Scope notes are written for a reader who has never seen the box and never will unless the note
persuades them to ask for it. Two or three sentences are usually enough. Name the people, the
places and the kind of record; say what years are covered thickly and what years are thin; and
mention anything a searcher would be glad to know in advance, such as a gap, a fragile item, or a
bundle that is written in shorthand. Do not summarise the contents as though writing a history of
the town.

Item-level listing, where every letter or photograph gets its own line, is done only for the collections
the committee has named. It multiplies the work by a factor of twenty or more and, for most boxes,
adds little that a good scope note does not already give. When an item-level list is made, it lives as a
separate document attached to the box entry rather than replacing it, so the summary view of the
whole collection stays readable to someone in a hurry or a searcher on the telephone.

The reference number is the only thing that must never change. Titles can be corrected, date ranges
narrowed, scope notes rewritten, but the number printed on the box, written in the register and
quoted in a researcher's footnote has to point at the same material for as long as the archive exists.
When two boxes turn out to belong together they are cross-referenced; they are never renumbered,
however untidy the result looks.

Every catalogue entry names the volunteer who wrote it and the month it was written. That is not a
matter of credit. When an entry turns out to be wrong, which happens, the quickest way to
understand the error is to ask the person who made it what they were looking at, and when a whole
run of entries shares a misunderstanding it helps to know they came from one hand in one season
rather than from everyone at once.
